speechtext:
I am not aware of any
regulation which prevents a man being

Supply-Dejence-Relief Camps
accompanied by a companion when he wishes to discuss a complaint he wants to make to the foreman.

Is there any regulation
that allows this? As the matter stands now and as it is definitely stated in the regulations, anything savouring of combination in the presentation of grievances is disallowed; the rules are very emphatic on that point. One of the first things that must be done, if we are to administer the camps with any degree of satisfaction to the men in them, is that they should be allowed to organize in such a way that they can properly present their grievances to the foreman. Moreover, after they are discharged from the camp they are never called before any board or committee to state their case. The superintendent, if the case comes before him, gets only the foreman's side of it; he never gets the man's side

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Can my hon. friend
prove that?

Supply-Defence-Relief Camps
"Personnel will be free to leave the work to accept other employment offered; they may be discharged 'for cause' and if so discharged will subsequently be ineligible for reemployment under the scheme."
That is one of the conditions for which some remedy must be provided.
"Free transportation will be given from place of engagement and return thereto on discharge-except for misconduct.
"The standard of rations shall be that prescribed for the army.
"No military discipline or training will be instituted; the status of the personnel will remain civilian in all respects.
"Officers in charge of projects are responsible for the care of the men placed under their supervision and it will be their object to ensure that their efficiency-mentally, physically and at their trades-is improved so that when conditions permit they may be returned to the economic life of the country well able to again take up their usual work. To assist in this, educational and instructional classes will be organized; recreation, amusements and games will be arranged'; every possible opportunity will be given to men to work at and to become proficient in their own selected trades.
"All concerned are reminded' that the funds are limited and that it is desired to care for the maximum possible number of men in need; that the possibility of obtaining additional funds depends to some extent on the value of the _ work done and, in consequence, that efficient direction and' strict economy in all matters are, therefore, of great importance."
A. McNaughton,
Major-General, C.G.S.
The committee finds that the first part of this arrangement has been lived up to by the Department of National Defence, that is in the matter of providing food, clothing and shelter for the men, but that the second part, that is of seeing to the psychological side of the men's lives, has not been lived up to. I will read from the report:
A period of eight months has elapsed since this policy was put into operation, and during that period your committee has kept in close touch with conditions in the camps and the difficulties confronting the administration. It has through direct personal contact with officials administering relief, as well as with men in the camps, obtained a great deal of information which has been carefully considered.
The conclusions 'arrived at are submitted as suggesting a constructive policy .acceptable both to the government and to the men, which whilst practical would not necessitate heavier financial outlay. In general we find that in the matter of accommodation, clothing, food, medical care, work and 'allowances, the Department of National Defence on behalf of the Dominion of Canada has fulfilled its obligations and carried out its promises and we are particularly impressed with the high standard of living in the camps and the moderate cost of the ration maintenance.
There is, however, a broader and, in the opinion of this committee, a more important aspect to the whole situation which cannot longer be ignored and must in any plan for
[Mr. Maclnnis.l
unemployment relief be recognized as the most important factor in the whole situation-we refer to the maintenance of morale and the recognition 'by the government that food for the mind is as important as food for the body and that healthy recreation in addition to the daily work is so essential as to need no further emphasis.
I quite appreciate the fact that the present Minister of National Defence has been administering his department for only a short time, and that even if he were anxious to do something towards reorganization he may not have had the time to give the matter the consideration it merits. I find however that speaking in this chamber on Friday evening last the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Sutherland), formerly Minister of National Defence, made this statement:
If the men are warm, if the clothing provided is good and the food substantial, I do not think there can 'be anything to complain of.
I wonder if the hon. member ever, heard the saying that man cannot live by bread alone. He requires something more than food, shelter and clothing. Animals can get along with limited requirements, but even with respect to animals, if we wish to obtain the best results we must treat them kindly and give them attention. Then, the minister went on to say:
The camps are not permanent; it is not as though the men were going to be there for some time and had to build up some system of rights.
As a matter of fact, so far as we can see at the present time the camps are permanent. That is one of the difficulties. The men feel when they go to the camps that there should be written over the doors of the camps the words: All hope abandon ye who enter here. There is no hope for the man going into a camp to-day; he may be in there for the next five years or possibly for the rest of his life. The minister cannot say, the government cannot say, and no hon. member in this chamber can say when the camps may be abolished. Continuing the report says:
It is our considered opinion that there are classes of single unemployed men for whom more or less permanent provision will have to be made and that failure to recognize this fact and plan accordingly will have serious effects on the whole situation. The presence of 5,000 single men in the city of Vancouver registered as unfit and homeless seems to justify this statement.
We 'believe that the whole situation should be surveyed throughout the dominion by a commission competent by reason of the experience of its personnel to advise the government as to the policy to be pursued.
When we were advocating a committee to investigate camps I was not aware that this report existed. I believe it goes considerably

Supply-Defence-Relief Camps
farther than the suggestions we made, and indicates that the whole governmental policy should be considered. The report continues:
The main points we desire to emphasize are as follows:
(a)	A work and wages scheme in lieu of the allowance system.
(b)	Coordination between the government employment services and the camp authorities.
(c)	Organization of recreational activities.
(d)	Regular periods of leave.
(e)	Segregation of age and youth within the camps.
(f)	Welfare committees of the men elected by the men in each camp.
(e) The necessity for suitable personnel.
Your committee has urged in the past the necessity for a work and wages scheme and is still of the opinion that this would largely diminish the present unrest in the camps, without extra cost to the government.
There are many problems due to the present basis of administration, connected with clothing, tobacco and snuff issues, and transportation which we think could be obviated by a wages system, and, most important of all, we think that such a system would help to preserve a man's self respect.
To arrive at a satisfactory basis of pay, it is suggested! that men should be required to work for a sufficient number of hours each week to enable them to earn at the minimum wage rate for unskilled labour enough to pay for theiT board, clothing, lodging and issues, an actual cost basis plus a cash surplus of not less than twenty cents per working day.
The committee feel that when skilled tradesmen or mechanics are used at their trades, the rate of pay should be increased and the hours reduced if necessary.
On several occasions complaints have been made to me, more particularly during the last session of parliament, to the effect that the department was using men skilled in various trades and giving them relief camp allowance pay.
Then a section of the report is headed "Coordination between the government employment services and the camp authorities." I shall not read the suggestions in detail, but would state briefly that the committee recommended very close coordination between the government employment service and the camps, because the men in the camps are away from the cities and for that reason are not in a position to look for work for themselves. Then the report continues:
There is no organization of games and recreation; books and magazines are circulated regularly to all camps, but this does not suffice, and proper supplies of recreational equipment such as footballs, soft balls, fishing gear, etc., should be provided. We are of the opinion that a sum of $4,000 annually would be sufficient for the men's needs in this respect and would go far towards preserving the morale of both old and young. Any expenditure of this character should be very carefully laid out; as there are miany articles such as softball bats and cricket bats which can be made by the men themselves. The cam-p visitors for
the iChureh Cooperative Camp iGouneil have reported the pleasure derived by the men in the camps and their gratitude for issues of sporting goods which were distributed in fifty camps of this province during the summeir of 1933 from private funds, and this committee regards the recognition of this need by the government as one of the most urgent problems in the administration of camp relief.
A man sent to camp tends to lose hope and to become resigned to his fate. He feels that he is forgotten as "disposed of." Before he reaches this mental state and as an outlet for his dissatisfaction he makes trouble and is a fruitful field for "red" propaganda. If a short period of leave were granted every two months to the nearest town, conditional on good behaviour, despondency would he diminished and the men would have something to look forward to. Periodic leave is necessary for the maintenance of morale.
More consideration might be given, by the camp management to the effect of unemployment and isolation in camp on the mental life of the men.
As a matter of fact may I say that my experience was that this factor was overlooked in the camps, the management feeling that if they supplied reasonably good food and sufficient clothing to keep the men warm, that was all they were required to do. I quote further:
Segregation of youth and age within the camp. In certain of the camp areas it has been stated that the blending of age and youth has been adopted with the idea that the older men would have a steadying effect on the younger. This is, in the opinion of the committee, an unwise policy.
I am told, but I have no proof of it, that there are rather unfavourable moral effects arising from the mixing of old and young men in these camps. Continuing:
Welfare committees of the men elected by the men in each camp.
That is what I would like particularly to impress upon the minister because I feel quite satisfied that no group of self respecting men can submit to discipline and accept orders in regard to matters over which they have absolutely no control and in which their opinion is not asked. Continuing to quote:
Committees or organizations of men within the camp areas are not officially recognized as they are considered to be subversive of discipline and order. Committees, however, do operate within the camp areas with or without tacit approval, and we ask the question: Is it better to have a properly constituted camp committee operating in the open, or a bush committee acting under a sense of grievance?
We recommend that more trust and confidence be placed in the men and that grievances are better ventilated in the open than suppressed. It should not be a difficult matter to devise a scheme whereby grievances may be heard, examined and dealt with in a satisfactory manner.

Supply-Defence-Relief Camps
I suggest to the minister that he give this particular section of the report his very serious consideration, as I am convinced that the carrying out of these recommendations would overcome many of the difficulties that now exist in the camps. I am convinced of that because I have worked with men and I know men, and I know how easy it is to get their cooperation when you go half way to meet them. Again quoting from the report.
The necessity for suitable personnel. We are of the opinion that the whole atmosphere of a camp depends on the personality of the camp foreman.
Your committee knows one camp where the foreman issues no restrictive orders, where the men have supported him in refusing to allow communists to come into the camp, and where no "bush'' committee exists.
In this camp the foreman leads his men in recreational activities, plays with them; he listens to their requests even though unable to grant them. In this camp there has been little or no trouble at any time.
This foreman has proved under two systems of relief, provincial and dominion, over a long period in one camp, that the human factor is all-important, and that men can be controlled and even made happy in adverse circumstances by the exercise of humanity, fellowship and tact.
We submit that what is needed in the camps is a positive program of work and welfare activities for the men in preference to a list of prohibitive orders.
We think that camp foremen as well as supervisors should be chosen as far as possible from men who have proved their worth in subordinate positions in camp administration.
This is along the line I suggested to the minister the other evening, that the man who makes a good foreman in a construction camp does not necessarily make a good foreman in a camp of this kind, which requires a different type of man altogether. Again quoting from the report:
Men expelled from camp. Under the regulations laid down by the Department of Militia and Defence a man may be summarily discharged for cause, and neither the department nor any other relief authority appears to have any further responsibility for his care.
Furthermore, it appears that there is no court of appeal to whom such a man may refer his case for reconsideration except this same department.
The committee is of opinion, in view of the possibility of unfair action by a camp foreman being sustained by his higher authority, that there should be set up an independent board to review such disciplinary action and make a final judgment on such cases.
I would also ask the minister to give his attention to that. I shall pass over the next part of the report, which refers largely to men in the cities, and come to the two concluding paragraphs:
[Mr. Maclnnis.l
In conclusion, this committee desires to place on record its considered opinion that a commission representative of the governments concerned should be appointed to coordinate the work of the various relief authorities at present caring for destitute persons, both married and single, as only by such means can some of the present anomalies and injustices be avoided.
The issues are so vast and so far-reaching in their effects on the men and women of future generations that nothing less than a complete control of the whole field of relief administration can prevent incalculable harm from being done to the moral and physical stamina of the nation.
All of which is respectfully submitted.
Then follow the names of the committee which I have already given. This I believe is a very reasonable repdrt. It has been issued for over a year now, since March, 1934, and yet the conditions in the camps, as far as the subject matter of this report is concerned, are worse than they were a year ago. I know that you cannot abolish these camps in a day or at a moment's notice, but until such time as the camps can be abolished I think this government and parliament should not rest until they have made conditions in the camps where the men now are, and may be for some considerable time, just as good as they can possibly be made. I hope the minister will give this matter his consideration and be able to report in the very near future that he has found it feasible to put some of these long-needed reforms into effect.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I cannot say that I have in front of me the report from which the hon. member has been reading,, but if it has been received in the department it certainly has been considered and considered most carefully.
I notice that one appeal the hon. member made was that we should keep in close touch with the Employment Service of Canada. I may inform him that we receive the men into the camps through the agency of the Employment Service of Canada.
My hon. friend read out a list of names of the people on the committee that produced this report, and I noticed there were several clergymen thereon. In the course of my remarks I shall draw the committee's attention to the report of another clergyman who has spent the last two and a half years travelling up and down British Columbia visiting these camps, because I think the committee may be interested in hearing his account of what he finds.
On a previous occasion when this matter was before the committee several statements were made by hon. members which I undertook to

Supply-Defence-Relief Camps
investigate. One of them was made by the hon. member who has just spoken (Mr. Mac-Innis). He referred to the ease of a cook in a camp who quit when told that he was exceeding the per capita allowance and instructed to cut down, and said that this cook had made reference to a still being operated by the supervisory staff, using camp supplies.

May I correct the minister? I did not say this cook referred to it. I said that a cook came in after this man quit, and the men in the camp found the still. That had no relation to the first cook at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Then it was two different people, one cook who was discharged for having given the men too much to eat, and another who made a statement with regard to a still in the camp.
No, it was the men themselves who made the statement in regard to the still.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Well, a man made a statement with regard to a still.
Amen.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
As these charges were vague I wrote to the hon. member a day or so after the incident was mentioned in the committee and asked him if he would be good enough to give me closer information so that the charges could be investigated. On March 7 the hon. member replied that the statement had been made by one of the relief camp workers by the name of Cumber. The hon. member went on to say that regardless of whether or not the statements were true, they were of such a nature in his opinion as to warrant an investigation. An investigation was made and it was found that this man Cumber has something of a record in British Columbia. He first came to the attention of the department when a request was received from Robert Macnicol, secretary of the provincial command, Canadian legion, under date of December 5, 1934, that Cumber should be reinstated. The case was fully investigated at that time and on January 4 the following report was made:
He was in project 25 from 23rd August, 1933, to 22nd September, 1933, when he was discharged for refusing to work. A week later he was sent to camp 227 where he stayed from 1933 to 7th March, 1934. While in camp 227 be was prominent in three strikes, but worked in the background, not giving the foreman of the camp any specific grounds to discharge him until he finally came into the open in a strike on 7th March, 1934, when he was discharged 'as one of the ringleaders. The activities of the
leaders in this strike unfortunately resulted in the discharge of between 30 to 40 men. The superintendent of the group to which camp 227 belong considers Cumber is one of the most dangerous types of agitators, and were he readmitted to any camp he would make trouble by his clever undercover methods.
After his discharge on 7th March, 1934, Cumber applied for reinstatement twice, but his applications were not approved. His second application was made on 23rd October, 1934, and' this headquarters made further enquiries into his ease before refusing his application again. However, Cumber did not wait for a reply but applied for relief under an assumed name (E. Tuckett) at the same time making a false statutory declaration that he had not previously been in any relief camp, and was sent to camp 209 on 6th November, 1934, and was later recognized as Cumber. Apparently he realized he had been recognized for he left at his own request on 20th November. Action is being taken to institute proceedings against him for obtaining relief by false pretences.
In the March 7 issue of the Relief Camp Worker appeared the following:
Acting Secretary out on bail. Huge campaign to bring pressure on the authorities launched.
Vancouver, March 5th.-Comrade E. Cumber, the acting secretary of the union, appeared in court yesterday at New Westminster where he had been transferred from Hope. He is charged with obtaining relief under an assumed name.
It appeared to me to be useless to endeavour to get any more information that could be relied upon from that source, and the investigations were discontinued. I think it is quite evident to hon. members of the committee that agitators of this description exist in all these camps.
Not all.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: With very few exceptions.
Except Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I think I will be able
to show the hon. member that they are pretty widely spread. They appear to exist only for the purpose of agitating and it is interesting to note that in communication after communication appears the statement that the majority of men in the camps do not want to be bothered with the agitators. They want to be allowed to continue to do what work they can do and on frequent occasions they have intimated to the agitators that their presence in the camp was not wanted. Considerable correspondence has been received on this matter by myself and by hon. members. Different citizens who have paid voluntary visits to these camps inform us that the conditions are good. They state that they do not consider the complaint of the agitators that grievances should be handled by a committee is a valid one. The

Supply-Defence-Relief Camps
statement has been made on the last two occasions on which this matter was discussed, particularly by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Maclnnis), that these men would not make complaints because they dreaded being discharged, but I submit that this statement is not founded on fact. There are a number of instances on record where individuals in the different camps across Canada have made complaints to the foremen. Some of these complaints have been carried to the superintendent but they have all been handled in a sympathetic and tactful manner. Time and time again certain things have been adjusted and methods have been altered to the entire satisfaction of the man complaining. But the agitators still exist.
I should like to direct the attention of the committee to a statement which appeared in The British Columbian of March 13. The Reverend G. H. Finlay has devoted himself for the last two and a half years to the spiritual needs of these camps. He has visited many of the camps and has made short stays in some of them. The article reads:
In the two and a half years I have been visiting the camps, I have never found the food served disappointing, either in quantity or quality, despite whatever criticisms has been offered by speakers or wild statements appearing in the press.
The men in the camps are well off. The camps are comfortable, sanitary conditions are well looked after, there is first aid equipment and each camp is vieited by a medical man twice a week. In fact the provision made for the men in the camps is immensely better than for many families on relief in New Westminster and Vancouver.	_
Men accommodated in the relief camps in the Fraser Valley, Mr. Finlay said, come from every province in Canada, with scores of others from the British Isles. They represent a crosssection of the average citizenship of British Columbia or any other part of Canada. The troublesome element is in just about the same proportion as in a city of a similar number of inhabitants.
The relief camps were not started with the idea that they were a solution of the present economic difficulties. They are not permanent, but are just a "port in a storm", a temporary shelter, established to save men from dying in the ditch and to give them a chance to take care of their health.
There is dissatisfaction in the camps. But the dissatisfaction is purely a mental trouble, caused through discontent and the lack of any apparent hope for the future and the inability of the men to find an outlet for their ambitions. The dissatisfaction is not with the camps themselves, but with the system which brought the camps into being.
The work the men are called upon to perform is merely exercise, Mr. Finlay said. No attempt is made by the officers in charge "to push them". Speaking of the officials he said:
"I have never seen a better class of men than those in charge of the Fraser Valley camps. They are men who know how to handle men and some are more like fathers than bosses."

Referring to the malcontents, Mr. Finlay asserted that much of the trouble in the camps was caused by only two per cent of the total number of men accommodated. This minority believes that revolution is the only solution of the present difficulties and are determined to make the camps impossible. They refuse to work and no camp officials can tolerate them under their care; hence the blacklist. It is impossible for the average citizen to form an opinion on any debatable question that arises in the camps unless both sides are heard. In the past, Mr. Finlay said, only the disgruntled men have been heard, as the officials do not make a practice of stating their side of the case.
"Any stories of downright unfairness or ill-treatment have been grossly exaggerated and in many cases are wholly untrue," the speaker declared.
When a strike was called during the winter, only fifteen per cent of the men in the valley camps participated. The remaining eighty-five per cent, although discontented over economic conditions, had no complaint about the camps and refused to take part in the strike.
The statements made by this reverend gentleman and published in The British Columbian are statements which could well have 'been made by officials of the department. But surely they come with added force to hon. members of this committee as coming from a clergyman who has made it his duty to visit these camps for the purpose of studying the welfare of the men in the camps and so reporting. There is no question that the agitators exist. I think it would be desirable for me to draw the committee's attention to one or two pieces of information out of many which have come into the department in recent weeks.
I have under my hand a copy of some propaganda which has been circulated through the camps by subversive organizations whose one object is the destruction of law and order in this country, and who see, in the breaking up of the camps and the return of the men to the conditions of misery in the larger centres of population, a means through which their destructive purpose may be achieved. This is a copy of a sheet published in Calgary, head office given, the name of the secretary given, dated March 3. It is headed: "Relief camp workers' union, Alberta section." It was picked up in one of the Ontario camps. It begins:
To all workers in relief camps.
I will not read it all, but the first sentence reads:
The time has come to take some action to improve the position of the single unemployed workers.
It goes on with three or four inches like that, and then comes to the setting up of the camp committees:
On arrival in camp it should be the duty of all workers who realize the need of organization to set up a camp committee, in case

______________Supply-Dejence-Relief Camps
one does not exist. This committee would comprise a small group of active workers. They would make a survey of camp conditions, note the immediate grievances and the attitude of the men toward organization. After a plan of work is decided upon, the committee can draw others around it.
And so on. That apparently is circulating in the camps throughout Canada. This circular describes the method of organization of these camp committees. The camp committees desire to find out which of the men are useful soil in which agitation can be seeded so that at a given time when the opportunity is ripe they may act in a concerted fashion in the direction they desire to go. There is nothing particularly new about this method; for I would remind hon. members that it is extraordinarily similar to other documents which we read in 1917 at the time of the breakup of Russia, and they were used again in extraordinary similarity at the time the German fleet went to pieces and bloodshed ensued. Further than that, there is evidence in the department of a widespread and well organized plot, that on a given date in the near future these subversive organizations will attempt the destruction of the camps throughout Canada. Needless to say the necessary steps to safeguard against any such contingency have been taken.
It is interesting to note that definite instructions have been sent by the organizations to their agents in our camps, that when the uprising takes place it will be possible to accomplish their end. I have in my hand a copy of the Relief Camp Worker, which was published on March 19 and is the organ of the relief camp workers' union, British Columbia district. The address of its office in Vancouver is printed and at the top of the page is "Conference Number" and at the bottom of the page, "Not a man left in camp, April 4." Again, I will not read it; there is a good deal of it-four pages of it. On the front page I note that it says:
On April 4 British Columbia and Alberta will be the scene of the greatest attempt by the camp workers to emancipate themselves from the yoke that predominated in the dim past.
And lower down:
Let us go forward in the coming struggle with the only weapon that gets results; that is, organized militant action; no dallying with these political heelers whose promises are not worth the paper they are written on, but forward with a determination to show the people of B.C. that the camps are a menace to the youth.
Further on:
Start by building such a solid organization on a district basis that there will not be a 92582-144
man left on April 4. Cooperate with your district organizer and look to your mail contract.
I think that is evidence sufficient to demonstrate that we are face to face with a definite organization of men who are desirous of raising trouble so considerable that it may be handled but with difficulty. I need not repeat the arrangements under which the dominion government came into this relief picture; I have stressed them again and again. When the dominion government came into it, it was for the purpose of assisting the provinces to handle a certain load which they had to carry, and it was arranged that the Department of National Defence should be given the task of carrying out the work. The reason that was done was that under the Department of National Defence Canada is divided into certain districts. In each of these districts there is a certain organization including engineer services. There are store services and supply services. It was not necessary therefore to set up a whole piece of new machinery throughout Canada to carry out this rather extensive piece of work, and so it was handed to the Department of National Defence. That department has carried it out, always with that idea in view, that we were there to give the assistance laid down by agreement with the provinces in connection with work arranged with the provinces and with machinery lent by the provinces, in order to give food, shelter and certain other things to the single, homeless unemployed in need of relief and who were physically fit.
Certain criticism was made-rather strong criticism-on the last occasion these estimates were being discussed, of the wording of certain regulations. But let me remind the committee that regulations are enacted for the purpose of handling the work carried out in these camps. The law abiding man in the camp does not fall foul of the regulations. If he has complaints to make he makes them and they are handled to the best of their ability by the several ranges of authority, from foreman up to headquarters. But as we know that we are dealing with agitators and as we know that we have to make arrangements that law and order shall be preserved not only in the camps but in the countryside, it is necessary that regulations be formulated to direct the foremen and superintendents how to handle anything in the nature of roughness or revolution which may crop up. I have to assure hon. members of the committee that we have knowledge what I have read here is actually extant in our



Supply-Defence-Relief Camps
midst to-day, and proper regulations and arrangements have been made to cope with the difficulty.
Mr. MaeINNIS: After I made the statement about the evidence given in regard to the still in the camp, the minister wrote to me asking for further information. I gave him that information, furnished him with the name of the person who made the statement, and described the circumstances in which the statement was made. I now find that he tracked down the individual who made the statement but did not track down or try to track down the still or those who were operating it. The reason he gave for not doing that was that the man was supposed to be an agitator. Evidently everyone who disagrees with conditions in the camp is an agitator. But let me tell the members of the committee that the world owes a great deal to agitators. Without agitators there would be no progress, so let us put its proper value on agitation.
The article that the minister read from The British Columbian is not essentially different from the report I read; in fact it is practically the same thing. They agree that conditions in the camps are in some respects all right, but more is required than mere food, clothing and shelter. Then the minister says only two per cent of the men are agitators or have leanings that way. Surely then if there is proper organization in the camp the other ninety-eight per cent will not follow the misguided two per cent. The fact is that there is no agitator but injustice. Do away with injustice and agitators will find nothing to thrive on. I have information in regard to the agitation that was carried on in the summer of 1930 before this government came into office, what was said about the government of that day, comparing the present leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) to Judas. Who organized the unemployed in Regina?

Who referred to him as Judas?
Mr. MaeINNIS: The present Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) when he was an agitator. Who organized the unemployed at Regina and gave them buttons to wear in the lapels of their coats?

The Tories.
Mr. MaeINNIS: Chickens will come home to roost. Now we are not going to meet this situation by suppression. We should meet it by removing the injustices, and then, as I have said, agitators will find nothing to do.
[Mr. Stirling.!
Carried.

Before the item carries I should like to ask the minister if it is the policy of his department to send around officers to investigate conditions in the camps, not merely those in British Columbia but in other parts of the dominion. Also, assuming these investigators are making rounds of the camps, whether their reports are submitted to his department, and if he has any such reports with him at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Officials of the department are constantly travelling around to the camps. I have not any collected reports here. Their reports come in from time to time and close check is kept on them. But as Canada is divided into districts the reports are made to district headquarters, which in turn report to the department. There is no book of reports like this that I can refer to, but the reports are continually coming before us.

Has the department made
any investigation of the camp at Lac Seul?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Yes, there have been
rather extensive reports on Lac Seul.

I would like some information in regard to conditions in that camp. I have had complaints in regard to the inefficiency of the whole administration there. I would like to know the total cost of the work done in that camp and also something in regard to what has been accomplished.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
My information is that
up to some months ago there was a considerable amount of trouble and disaffection at Lac Seul, but for the past five or six months the camp has quieted down to a very considerable extent, and since I have been in this position I have not had reports of any unfortunate happenings at Lac Seul.

Could the minister inform
the committee What the official reports were in regard to the cause of the dissatisfaction and trouble in that camp?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Total expenditures to September 13, 1934, were $664,373. I am not in a position at the moment to answer my hon. friend's question, but I shall be glad to report to him by letter.

My information which has
come to me from more than one source, is that this is a most extravagantly conducted camp, and that the work, although done by the cheapest labour available, could have been done for a very small proportion of the amount that has been spent by the department. The

Supply-Defence-Relief Camps
reports I had, which came from a reliable source, included for example the statement that four carloads of beef were destroyed; they had been there so long that they were totally unfit for human consumption. Does the minister know anything in regard to that?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No, I cannot corroborate or deny that statement, but it certainly will be looked into. We must remember that Lac Seul is an isolated place. The work was undertaken in accordance with the views of both province and dominion, to achieve a certain purpose, the clearing of the shore at the present water level of Lac Seul and to the height to which the water will rise. It will be a feeder for a future power plant, a work that will be of advantage to that part of Canada at a later day. If men are placed in camp in an isolated place like that, however desirable the work that may be accomplished, it is probable that it will not be done as economically as if it were close to centres of supply. I think I can meet the contention of the hon. member with regard to enormous extravagance, and I shall be happy to do so if he wishes it.

Can the minister say how
much land was cleared there?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No, I am afraid I have not that detail here.
How many men are employed at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I am reading from the list which I tabled earlier this month. In the Lac Seul camps there were the following labourers on February 28:
