Besides clearing land, what other work are these men doing?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: They are clearing the land around the lake.

What other work are they
doing?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That is the main workclearing the foreshore.
So far, then, almost two-thirds of the million dollars has been expended in clearing the land at that point.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I can describe the work in much greater detail on a later occasion. I could not even tell the hon. member offhand the size of Lac Seul. If it is a big enough lake, the sum is not very large.

Have regulations been passed recently, especially with regard to the relief camp at Trenton, that the men employed there shall be deprived of their twenty cents a day allowance on wet days or days on which they do not work?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: : The regulation hitherto has been that the allowance of twenty cents is paid on days that some work is done.
Only on days that work is done?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes.

In that case may I inquire of the minister why it is called an allowance? Evidently, according to the statement of the minister, it is money paid for work done, but on several occasions he has referred to it as an allowance. I do not suppose there is very much use in pressing these objections, since the minister has declared himself satisfied with the relief camps, their function, operation, the personnel running them, and so forth. I also regret that he has seen fit to olass all those who object to conditions in relief camps as agitators. In any representations I have made to him I have been very careful to see that they were based only on facts presented to me by respectable and responsible bodies of citizens, one of them, for example, the Calgary city council. I sincerely trust the minister will not describe that body as inspired by agitators. I also hope he will not suggest that the board of the Vancouver council of social agencies is to be described as a radical, agitating body, or one inspired by motives such as those implied in the letters, pamphlets and statements the minister put on record in the closing part of his remarks. I have had complaints from many sources in regard to these matters, but have refrained from taking up any except official complaints. Interestingly enough, the official complaints registered coincide identically with those presented in this house by other hon. members and all of them ask exactly the same type of redress. They ask first for permission to the men in camps to have their own government, as it were, such as I suggested to the minister is the practice in universities, of course always subject to the general regulations of a superintendent which are necessary for proper procedure. Further, they should have a complaints committee. I would suggest that if the government were

Supply-Defence-Relief Camps
wise, they would go further and inaugurate sports committees. In other words, there would thus be a devolpment of self respect and self government in those camps; that would be the finest protection against the danger that the minister attempted to place before the committee, the danger of organized revolt.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: May I interpose a remark at this point? The hon. member surely does not want to suggest there are not sports committees and social committees in those camps?

All I have to say is this: I read from the regulations. By the way, I may say that I do not hold Brigadier-General D. W. B. Spry responsible for them; they quite clearly emanated from headquarters, but these are the regulations that went out under his signature:
(a) One of the fundamental and most necessary rules for the administration of unemployment relief camps is to forbid anything bearing the appearance of combination to obtain redress of alleged grievances. Appeals for redress by means of any document bearing the signature of more than one complainant, or by organized committees combining to make a complaint are strictly forbidden.
That is quite clear; there can be no dispute about that at all. Furthermore, since that point has been raised again, I would like to know upon what authority even the Department of National Defence, merely because it has the function of operating what is normally a civil camp, a relief camp, has undertaken to take away from those people their civil liberties. Note regulation (f):
No application or complaint should ever be made to the civil power, except through the camp foreman or with his sanction.
Frankly, that is going just a bit too far, as I said the other evening. However I do not want to strain the point or continue this discussion unnecessarily, but I, would like to point out to the minister that in the Calgary Albertan of March 23, that is of Saturday last, there appeared the following dispatch:
At its last two meetings Calgary city council has expressed opposition to the relief camp regulations which drew fire in the House of Commons Friday night.
The council passed a motion requesting information on the following four points:
1.	Rescind "vicious" regulations regarding appeals to outside sources.
2.	Permit group organizations and grievance committees.
3.	Send no men to camps which were not fully ready for occupancy.
4.	Provide additional recreational facilities.
Organizations opposed to the relief camp
principle, and protesting alleged grievances, have called' a convention in Calgary April 5.

It is not of much use, but I would again raise my voice in protest against these regulations.
I also ask the minister to take into serious, nay, into more than serious consideration, the effect on character, on morality, on the general fibre of the people in these camps. I have complaints that I intend to send to the minister in writing-they are not the kind that I care to give expression to on the floor of the house-with regard to the moral conditions in those camps, where 'teen-age boys and older men are all mixed up together, where because of distance from centres of population they are separated entirely from the normal enjoyment of an ordinary life. They are not permitted to go into those places for more than two days in, I think, a month. They have therefore no opportunity to hunt for jobs for themselves or to seek relief from the oppressive routine of camp work. I want to be accurate on this point; is it two days a month?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I think it is two days a
month.

I have complaints on that point, and also complaints that the comfort funds, as they call them, in some camps are not being properly administered. I am told the dormitories in the Trenton camp are overcrowded. In the dormitories occupied by the air force men there are only five beds, the men in the employment camp having sixteen. The communication I have before me indicates that sixty-four men on one floor use one bathroom. The correspondent states:
I think that we should receive more assistance in trying to get a job. As it is, the government seems to put every possible obstruction in our way, the chief of which is the limited time allowed for leave. We can only take a maximum of two days. If we go for longer than that we must check out. How can we hitch hike and look for a job in two days from a place as isolated as this? If we check out we have no certainty of getting back. In any case we lose any and all of the provileges and position we may have worked into and up to during our original term. If we return we are set back right at the beginning at the pick and shovel, without any precedence or prestige to our name.
Of course under present conditions I do not know where the poor beggars would find jobs, but still we know that hope springs eternal in the human breast, and I suppose they will continue to drift in the hope that conditions may have improved and that they may have an opportunity to do something.
I have received another complaint to the effect that skilled labour is being paid no more than unskilled labour on relief work. I believe the minister knows this fact. Truck drivers,

Supply-Defence-Relief Camps
mechanics, carpenters, machinists, stenographers and so on are all paid the same, namely twenty cents per day. That is bad enough where there is no comparison possible between that rate of pay and other rates, but unfortunately in the camp at Trenton there is an intermingling between relief project men and air force employees, with the result that anomalies are inescapable. The correspondent states:
We have seen first class mechanics taken from our ranks to work side by side with air force mechanics for twenty cents a day. while the air force mechanic doing less work and being less skilled received his full stipend. We have had carpenters working for twenty cents a day beside carpenters brought in from outside working for forty cents an hour. Last summer while we were constructing a cement sidewalk from the camp to the village three different systems of relief were in operation side by side: the provincial highway scheme paying twenty-five cents an hour, the municipal scheme paying (I believe) forty cents an hour, and the project gang, doing just as much work as the other two, getting twenty cents a day.
Obviously under those circumstances the minister must not be surprised if there is some dissatisfaction and if indeed there may even be some British citizens there who have enough of the old British spirit in them to resent such treatment and to agitate against it. He continues:
The twenty cents a day wage and several of the routine and disciplinary injustices inflicted on us are due to the fallacy of calling us unemployed. Obviously when a man works eight hours a day he is no longer unemployed.
They are really in the camps and employed. It may be that they are employed only for their clothing-or part of it-their board and twenty cents a day.
I do wish we could arrive at a solution of this problem. In spite of the minister's endorsation of these regulations I am convinced that in his heart of hearts he does not endorse them. I believe he is as much satisfied as any hon. member in this committee that there has to be an improvement of conditions. Some action must be taken to stimulate the self respect of these men and to help them to hold themselves steady until conditions improve, if ever. I would ask the minister at this stage not to harden his heart against the necessity for speaking strongly about the rigidity of the military discipline originating at headquarters in Ottawa. These people in Ottawa doubtless have their place; the type of man in question is necessary for certain kinds of work, but certainly their work is not that of governing a body of civilians who, through no fault of their own, are placed in a position where at least
temporarily they are subject to the Department of National Defence. I suggest that there be a complete relaxation of disciplinarian measures to a degree where these men may be allowed their complaints committee and given greater recreational facilities. The purchase of footballs or softballs would not require a great deal of money, and I believe the government could make the expenditure without endangering its financial standing. I am sure an expenditure of that kind would be appreciated. A little greater cooperation between the superintendent and the men might be recommended by the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Certainly these matters
will be looked into. But the minister who could give a ready answer to the pages of criticism which have been read would have to be a superman. I cannot do it; it is impossible for me to do so. Consequently I am driven to ask this question:	Is it
quite fair to read stuff of that sort, to reel it off in committee where an answer cannot be made, when it would have been quite possible to hand the information to the minister, in which event he would have had an opportunity to make inquiries? Three or four weeks ago I paid an interesting visit to Trenton upon which occasion I was shown everything. I did not consider that the men were crowded in their dormitories. My very clear recollection is that nothing like the condition described by the hon. member existed, and that nothing like the number of men mentioned by him had to share one bathroom. The air force employees and relief men were not working side by side. There were at least half a dozen carpenters, more electricians and more men in other trades who were receiving the ordinary trade wages obtaining in the neighbourhood, and who were assisted in their operations by the men on the twenty cent allowance. My hon. friend made the statement on the authority of a person who had communicated with him that the men were all jumbled together and that all received an allowance of twenty cents per day. That certainly is not the case at Trenton. However I shall be happy to have the matter looked into and a detailed reply given to the hon. member.

It happened to be my privilege to go through these camps, and I am at a loss to understand hon. members opposite. If they have never been through relief camps I would advise them to go and observe the conditions. The statement I am about to make can be borne out by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River who, I believe, is in his seat. While in his section of the country I visited a camp at Vermilion Bay, and I can
225S
Supply-Defence-Relief Camps

assure hon. members that the conditions in that camp were better than the conditions which existed in Camp Hughes from 1915 to 1918. I would like to tell hon. members opposite that when I entered the cookhouse door I saw a huge pan of doughnuts of the very best quality sitting on the stove and being prepared for supper. The hon. member for Vancouver South took exception to an article I read a short time ago. This evening I should like to make a correction concerning that letter which, on that occasion, I indicated was from a young man in one of the camps. The letter I have before me at this time states:
You can certainly tell Mr. Maclnnis that everything the boy said was perfectly true and I have been away from there six months or more. Apparently after reading Mr. Maelnnis's speeches he could never have had much experience with the interior decoration of a bunk-house. The boy was mistaken in so far as the horse blankets are concerned. They are not horse blankets; they are regulation army issue.
The family said after I came back to Winnipeg that I was spoiled in so far as my eats are concerned. When I read the speeches in there I simply could not stop sending you this letter. I hope you are in the best of health.
I have another letter here from the superintendent of a park that has 650 men in one of these camps; they get nothing but the very best. There must be something wrong with my hon. friends over on the other side of the house. They must be saying these things for some purpose. At the camp at Vermilion, for instance, and I am sure the hon. member for that district will bear me out in this statement, the men are fed the very best, are housed the very best, and are living under the very best conditions. Of course it is a camp; it is not the Royal York hotel or the Chateau Laurier. What do you expect? If it is any information for the hon. gentleman, personally I would turn these men loose and tell them to go out to work. There is plenty of work for them on the land. The farmers in my constituency are asking for them. I just got a letter to-day from a farmer in my constituency who offered one of these men 830 a month. I know that farmer very well, and I know he would treat the man well, but the man stayed with him just one day. He left because the farmer called him for breakfast at six-thirty in the morning. These men are spoiled, and if you keep on pampering them and feeding them with the very best of food, such as the minister gives them, you will never get rid of them. Turn them out and let them work the same as we had to do as pioneers. Those of us who were out

west in the early days never got such pampering nor lived under such good conditions. I do not know the object of hon. gentlemen who are making these complaints, but I have my own idea. If they will go into the camps and see the conditions I am sure they will change their minds. I have been through the camps at Vancouver and New Westminster, and I did not see anything to complain of. The hon. member for New Westminster is in his seat, and he knows very well that these men are well fed and that everything is all right. There is nothing wrong in the camps. They are comfortable and everything is of the very best, unless conditions have changed since I visited them not long ago. I certainly would recommend that hon. gentlemen go through the camps and look at them for themselves unbiased, and then I am sure they will come to the same conclusion that I have come to.

I have a communication dated March 23, 1935, and if the minister will assure me that the person who sent me this letter will not in any way be discriminated against for doing so I shall be glad to hand the communication to the minister. I ask for that assurance, because sending this letter is directly against the regulations of the department.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I shall be delighted to do what the hon. member suggests.

On that understanding I will let the minister have the communication. In reply to the hon. member for Marquette, I may say this correspondent states that the meal allowance is seven cents, or twenty-one cents per day for the three meals. I know from my own little experience in providing meals, not exactly in camps, that seven cents will not provide a very sumptuous sort of meal. This man further complains about the diet, and there are other complaints worse than that. One is that they have found in these camps a shortage of food. I do not know whether the shortage of food is due to the insufficiency of the meal allowance of twenty-one cents a day for the men who work in the camps, or whether it is due to a certain amount of pilfering that may be going on in the camp, but this man writes that there is a shortage of sugar, and he believes it is due to the fact that it is taken away in order to make home brew for the camp staff. There have been many complaints along that line. But the most important complaint this man makes is that there is a smouldering resentment against what is termed the slave conditions in the camp. I am going to hand this

Supply-Defence-Relief Camps
communication to the minister and I would ask him to look into these complaints. There is a large number of men, I believe, employed in this camp, and the complaints are along the line of those that have already been brought to the attention of the committee.
There is one further question I would ask of the minister. The last time this matter came before the committee, a week ago to-night, the minister said that he would deal sympathetically with the request that had been made by the hon. member for Vancouver South that the men employed in these camps should receive their indemnity of twenty cents a day for their services whether the weather is fine or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The hon. member asks
me whether I will deal sympathetically with the request that he has made. I may inform him, Mr. Chairman, that I have begun to deal.

I have
visited two of these camps. One of them is located in my own constituency. Prior to the establishment of these camps the city in which I reside operated a camp at the exhibition grounds, and they were quite unable to run it as efficiently as the camp is being run today under the department. As a result a lot of agitators and communists got into the camp in the city. The police tried to take fifty of them out one day and send them to another camp, but they refused to go, and as a result a riot broke out and Captain Sampson, who had bottles and bricks and everything else thrown at his horse, was killed. That was in the city of Saskatoon. Now there is a camp being operated by the department at Dundurn, thirty miles from where I live, and it has been my privilege to be there on several different occasions. I have talked with the men, and by and large they are all very well satisfied. They are well housed and well treated; there is no question about that. One day three men were thrown out of the camp because they refused to abide by the regulations. They were agitators trying to create trouble and a disturbance among the men in the camp. There were some fourteen hundred men in the camp at the time. These three men came back to Saskatoon and placed their troubles before some citizens, and a delegation of these people came to see me. They had not made inquiries as to the offences for which- these men were thrown out; they simply came to me weeping and wailing because of the so called bad treatment these men had received. A day or two later these three men who had been thrown out of the camp called on me and told me a great tale of woe. I
must say that I did not receive them with outstretched arms or anything of that kind. Then these three men went to the chief of police and demanded beds in the police station. They did not get them. Finally they went to the Salvation Army, where they stayed. The next day I succeeded in getting a friend of mine who had a contract to take out railway ties in the constituency of my hon. friend from North Battleford to give these three men a job. I telephoned the chief of police and said, "You had better round them up and see if they want to work." He rounded them up and informed me that they did not have proper clothing. I asked him to inquire how much it would cost, and he bought sixty dollars' worth of clothes for them, which I paid for. They were sent out to the tie camp and given a job, but three days afterwards the mounted police were called in and these men were taken out of the camp, and eventually one of them found himself located in the gaol at Prince Albert. They were just communist agitators. They did not want to work.
There is another camp I have visited in Prince Albert national park. Several hundred men have been located there for a number of years. I went through the bunkhouses, the dining rooms and kitchen, and found them all in excellent condition. Two or three other men and myself spent a day or two at this park. We were in bathing at a spot some distance from the beach where most of the people live and three men came down to water some horses. We got talking to these fellows and they told us how delighted they were at having been able to get in the camp. The camp was about to be closed for the summer. They said they had been very well treated by the officials. It would almost seem as if British Columbia has a peculiar type of citizen, they have so much trouble out there with these agitators. There does not seem to be the same trouble in other camps. If these men would abide by the rules of the department I think they would find everything all right. Generally speaking, they are architects of their own misfortune. I think the department is to be commended for the manner in which they have handled this very difficult task and, on the whole, the men in the camps are to be commended for the manner in which they have handled themselves.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Administration, $359,000.

What is the explanation for the increase of $41,000?
Supply-National Defence

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: This is made up of pay and allowances for defence headquarters which are necessary because of a change in bookkeeping. Seven officers are being transferred from the permanent force, one of whom is employed on unemployment relief. There will also be allowances for the extra day for leap year. Instead of these staff officers being paid under the vote for the permanent force, they will now be paid from this vote, which is considered the proper place. That accounts for $30,700 of the increase. Transportation, travelling and removal expenses incidental to completion of staff appointments account for $5,000.

I notice the vote
for the permanent force is increased from $4,910,034 to $4,964,700. If the minister is taking $30,000 from the vote for the permanent force and transferring it to the vote for administration, the permanent force vote should be reduced by that amount.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Shall I deal with that
now or wait until we reach the permanent force vote?
I think this would be the proper place to deal with it.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The explanation is as
I have given, that these officers are now paid under administration. When we reach the permanent force vote I shall be glad to give an explanation then or I can give it now if the hon. member desires.
It would save time to give it now.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
This estimate is based
on a strength of 332 officers and 2,988 other ranks, also six officers of the non-permanent active militia attached for duty and 31 civilian employees.
May I interrupt? The minister is simply giving a general explanation of the vote. I do not want him to go to that trouble because that is not what I want.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: If the hon. member will permit me, I am just reaching the explanation he wants. The increase over 1934-35 is iix officers and eight other ranks.
Is that an increase in the permanent force?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Could we stay on the vote for administration?
How many officers?

I do not understand the explanation given by the minister. A

minute ago he told us that seven officers of the permanent force had been transferred from the permanent force to administration. 'If the vote for administration has been increased by $30,000, the vote for the permanent force should 'be reduced by the amount necessary for the salaries of these officers who have been transferred.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That is the explanation I have given. It has been considered necessary to augment the permanent force by that small number and the staff officers will in future be paid from the administration vote.

I am sorry but I do not understand the explanation. The minister stated that seven or eight officers of the permanent force, whose salaries had been paid from the permanent force vote, were being transferred and their salaries would now be paid out of the administration vote. The salaries for these officers cannot be provided for both in the administration and in the permanent force votes; if one is increased the other should be decreased.
Is the minister making a further explanation?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No.
Can the minister state the officers who are being transferred?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The increased amount is to cover the following appointments now being paid from permanent force vote:
Staff officer, medical services,
Assistant director, personal services,
Assistant director, organization,
G 2 training,
Assistant director, intelligence,
A.A. & Q.M.G. (unemployment relief),
Artillery liaison officer, R.C.A.F.
These positions are usually held by a major or senior captain and the units to which these officers belong are without the services of their corresponding ranks. The result is that other officers of lower rank are carrying out their regimental duties but cannot receive the appropriate rank or pay for the responsibilities they are forced to assume.
Do I understand that this is really an addition to the staff?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: These are transfers from the permanent force to administration.
An addition to staff by transferring regimental officers to staff appointments; is that it?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Hitherto these officers have been paid out of the permanent force

Supply-National Defence
vote and it has been considered more desirable that they should be paid out of the administration vote.
And they will perform the same duties which they performed when they were paid out of the permanent force vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes.
Is there an addition to the staff?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
No, except that one now working on unemployment relief.
Sir EUGENE FISiET:	I am afraid both
the minister and even my colleague, the former Minister (Mr. Ralston), are under a misapprehension. In the past these officers were paid from the permanent force vote. They were acting in a certain capacity, perhaps on the staff, but I understand that the payment of their salaries will now be made from the administration vote and that new staff appointments are being created for them. The minister has just stated what they were and he adds that they were transferred from tihe permanent force vote to administration because the department could not pay them adequate salaries for the work they did. I submit therefore that new staff appointments are being created.

I must protest against this militia vote which has appeared in the estimates year after year. I have protested against it before and I do so again. Here we have an increase of 8117,000. This week there was in Ottawa a meeting of all the mayors from the Atlantic to the Pacific protesting against the expense of keeping the unemployed in their cities. They told us it was impossible for them to continue handing out relief after the first of May; the taxes were so high that they could not raise sufficient money to support the unemployed. Yet here we find the militia service with an increased allowance of $117,000. Year after year the same thing happens: there is an increase in militia services, in police and in all forms of protection throughout the dominion. It is impossible for me to justify this vote. When we think of the number of people out of employment, when we think of the poverty and want throughout the country, on the farms and in the cities, when we remember that our boys last summer were going to militia camps on a holiday, drawing $1.10 a day, and furnished with new equipment, clothing and so on, while their fathers at home were not able to earn $1 a day, it seems to me that we are all wrong; we have gone astray-yes, as someone says,
we are all wet. This vote ought to be
reduced substantially year by year, and, I repeat, I cannot justify it on any ground. Those in the permanent service are being advanced every year just as if conditions were normal. The thing is ridiculous.

Do I understand the
minister clearly to say that there has been no creation of any new staff positions by this operation, except the creation of one new A.A.Q.M.G. for a particular purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That is my information; there have been no new staff appointments.

I take it that the position of staff officer, medical services, has always existed.
Mr. STIRLING He is performing this service but under a different name. That is the man.

It is not the man I am
talking about but the post.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The post is the same.
The officer is no longer called deputy director general of medical services; he is now called staff officer, medical services. The same man is doing the same work.

A new post is created
and the old post abolished?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes.

Will tlhe minister go
through the list and show us what the previous post was that is now represented by the post paid for under the administration vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That is the only one in the list that is changed.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Cadet services, $150,000.

How many cadets
were trained in the province of Quebec last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: There were 320 units, the same as the year before.
I mean the number that actually underwent training.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: As far as I am aware, that is the number that did train-320.
Will the minister give the number of cadets trained, by provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence

speechtext: In what provinces were there reductions?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: In all the provinces.
In what school are the cadets training in Saskatchewan?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I have not got it divided up according to units within the provinces. In Saskatchewan there were forty-one units on the last day of last year compared to forty-three the year before.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Contingencies, $31,500.

Why are there, practically speaking, three votes for contingencies? We have civil government, $45,000; we have contingencies,-I take it, for the permanent force-$31,000; and over and above that, in the vote for administration, there is provision for printing and stationery. I understand that the contingencies vote, so far as civil government is concerned, pays for expenses of civil printing in the department, and in the past it used to cover all printing and stationery expenditures for the whole department. Provision is being made here for the same kind of machinery in the administration vote. What is the purpose of these three different votes in one department?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The desire is that within each department the expenditures should fit with the work of that department. Shall I give the subdivisions?
I know them by heart, thank you.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The printing referred to
amounted to only $75.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Engineer services and works, $297,500.

I call the minister's attention to what is a very small matter as far as the total vote is concerned; I refer to the armoury accommodation at Yarmouth in my own constituency. The minister was good enough the other day to bring down a return showing the correspondence in connection with that matter. Summing up the return I think this is the situation: negotiations have been on foot for some time with the authorities of the United Church of Canada as to the possibility of utilizing a United church
TMr. Stirling.]
property there by way of either purchase or lease'. A definite price has been fixed as far as purchase is concerned, but as the correspondence discloses, no proposition has been received from the church authorities in response to a request for such proposition by way of lease. I do not know whether the minister has in mind continuing negotiations along that line or not. Pending that and pending some better general armouries accommodation there, I hope the minister will consider favourably a suggestion which is made in this return by the officer in command of No. 3 company, 6th Division Signallers, for some better accommodation for that unit. That does not mean that the 84th Field Battery, which is the other militia unit down there, does not need better accommodation, but it would appear from the correspondence that the commanding officer of the 84th battery is not particularly enthusiastic regarding the United church property; he indicates that it does not provide the fireproof accommodation which the battery would wish to have. But he does intimate that the signals in his opinion require better accommodation. There is a proposition on the file whereby signals may get separate accommodation outside the agricultural building-which is now being used by both units-in a building owned by E. H. Spinney at what appears to be a very small rent. At the present time the room for signals in the agricultural buildings is being paid for at the rate of $5 a month. The Spinney proposition would involve $10 a month instead of $5, and an expenditure of probably $500 in all to fit up the building. It would apparently give the signals very much better accommodation, as at present they have only one room in the agricultural building. I would ask the minister to go into the matter carefully, in the hope in the first place of providing better armoury accommodation all around, but in any case of providing at least better accommodation for the signals if it is found that there is no building sufficiently attractive to the military people to justify their recommendation.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I recall the matter that the hon. member has outlined. We are continuing to explore the possibilities of leasing.

I understand that
representations have been made to the minister in connection with armoury accommodation at Swift Current, Saskatchewan. Have any steps been taken towards furnishing better equipment along the lines of the suggestion that has been made?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
All that I can say is
that the Swift Current armoury suggestion is being given consideration along with all the other armouries which have been suggested throughout Canada.

Is there at present an
armoury at Calgary, and when does the minister expect to build that million dollar one which was passed in the public works program last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
If the hon. member will
recall, there is armoury accommodation at Calgary, which has been used for a considerable time by the permanent force. The barracks project which has been started on the plateau outside Calgary is for the purpose of restoring that armoury to the nonpermanent active militia, for whose purposes it was built.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
General stores, $837,800.

This item shows that
the total last year was the same, whereas last year's estimate show that the vote was only $667,800. Was there some supplementary vote last- year, or how is it the estimates this year show an increase over last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The difference is that
the hon. member has not added to the figure printed in last year's estimates the amount voted in the supplementary estimates of that year.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Non-permanent active militia, $2,000,000.

Would the minister tell
us what this item provides for as to the number of men who will be trained?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The estimates provide
unit training for the total 29,803 all ranks for a period of ten days.

Is it the same number
as last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Very much the same as
last year.

I see a $6,000 increase.
What is that for?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The increase for salaries and wages is necessary to cover adjustments in salaries of individuals who are exempt from the ten per cent deduction under the Salary Deduction Act. Provision for such adjustment was not made in the 1934-35 estimates.
Supply-National Defence

I should like to draw attention to a matter in connection with the militia department of this city, the 79th Queen's Own Cameron Highlanders. I ask the indulgence of the committee and the minister for doing this. As will be well understood, the Queen's Own Cameron Highlanders should have as their foremost band a pipe band. Surely the pipe band should be the premier band of a kiltie regiment, especially the Queen's Own Cameron Highlanders. My complaint concerning the Ottawa regiment is that all preference has been given to the bugle band in the matter of dress. I am asking the consideration of the minister because I know the pressure that has been brought to bear in this city that the bugle band shall stand out prominently, but I am in a position to offer practical criticism. This regiment has a tradition behind it, going back to 1710, I believe, or even further.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I shall be very glad to give consideration to anything relating to such a matter.
I suggest that the band be transferred to the sixth floor.
If there was as much sense on all floors as comes from the sixth, this house would be all right.

I understood the minister to say that this increase of $6,000 was to provide for restoration of cuts in certain salaries. Would the minister explain more fully who are exempt from this ten per cent cut and why?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I bad begun to read the explanation of the increase as it appeared in the general statement. There have been increases and decreases this year compared with last year; the $6,000 is the balance. I shall continue to read the note that I have.
Eleven new positions are included, three of these having been taken over from the public works department, and the balance for new armouries recently completed or at present under construction. When an armoury is completed the caretaking is taken over by national defence; while it was building it was in the hands of public works. Offsetting the eleven new positions are five which have been abolished. This is a plus and minus proposition, a give and take, but the balance is an increase of $6,000. The amount of training will 'be affected by restricting certain activities and limiting the number in attendance at instructional schools.
Supply-National Defence
I understood the minister to say that there were some men who were exempt from the ten per cent cut. Who are they?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I am afraid I have not with me the details as to who they were. If the hon. member wishes, I will obtain the information for him.
Are there any exempt and, if so, why are they exempt from the ten per cent cut?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Those that receive less than $1,000 had salary deductions made and then, if the hon. member will remember, those were restored to them. Provision has to be made to replace that which was taken from them before the legislation was changed.
A very small portion of the $6,000 is for adjustments. Apparently the larger portion is for the creation of new positions, is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Permanent force, $4,964,700.

There is a substantial increase in this item. Will the minister explain the increase, keeping in mind the fact that apparently, as pointed out by the hon. member for Rimouski, there should be reflected somewhere a $30,000 reduction owing to that amount having been transferred to administration.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
This increase is divided up as follows: there is an increase of $5,850 in connection with training, to enable training which has been extremely limited in the past to be carried out in a rather more extended form, so that the efficiency of the units will not foe impaired. I may say that running right through these estimates are evidences of the fact that this year we do not find the same necessity for drastic curtailment that existed for the last two years. During those two years when estimates were cut to the very bone, it is obvious that in matters such as stores and in other directions we have let stocks down pretty far. That applies to stores; it applies even to training; it applies in many directions. A slight effort has been made in most directions in these estimates to endeavour this year to catch up a little bit on what we had to let slip for purposes of economy in the past.
The seoond portion of the total increase comes under the heading of maintenance. This is another case where there are some increases and some decreases; for instance as

regards the allowance made for freight, express, cartage, we consider $1,000 will be sufficient. But for food and ice an increase of $8,000 is anticipated due to increases in prices of commodities. The same applies to forage; it also applies to fuel and gas, chiefly due to increased prices for coal and coke. There is an increase in laundry costs due to an increase in contract washing rates. There is an increase in cost of water due to an increase in rates. The decreases are based on expenditures for the coming year. It is anticipated that the amounts estimated under the several headings will meet requirements for 1935-36. In other words, the provision made for those particular items last year was a little more than the actual requirements.
What is the total increase under maintenance?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The increase is $22,249.
The third portion of the increase, $26,567, comes under the category "general." There again there are increases and decreases. The increases come under the heading of pay and allowances, due chiefly to an increase of six officers and eight other ranks in the strength of the permanent force over that for the fiscal year 1934-35, an additional day's pay having to be provided for leap year, also an increase in the number of married officers. Perhaps I should point out to the committee that for a good many years, I mean since the reorganization after the war, a certain establishment has been looked forward to in Canada. In the last year or two nothing in the nature of reaching out toward that establishment was possible. This year a little reaching out toward it has been considered possible, hence this small increase in the number of officers and other ranks.

Is the increase in the
number of regimental officers?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes.

Does this mean another
major or another captain or another lieutenant per battalion?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
They are junior officers
brought in. I cannot give the hon. member the exact units to which they are attached; I have not those details with me.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Royal Military College, $359,500.

What is the explanation
of the increase?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
This starts off with a
decrease of $1,990 in pay and allowances of military staff due to change in appointments

Supply-Defence-Naval Services
with replacements being made at lower rates of pay and allowances. As regards salaries of civilian personnel, sufficient funds are included to cover the restoration of one-half of the current ten per cent deduction, also statutory increases for the civilian members of the staff.

Are there any increases
in pay?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No.

Does the Minister of Finance concur in the statement made by the Minister of National Defence? I understood the estimates represented only ninety per cent of the total amount that was to be provided for salaries and that a special bill was to be introduced to provide for tihe five per cent increase, so I do not think the minister's explanation can be correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The general set-up was
that the estimates were prepared on the basis of last year's, which included the ten per cent deduction. There may be some exceptions in connection with this department.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No doubt my hon. friend heard me read a portion of-
Never mind; I am satisfied.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Naval Services-	.
To provide for the maintenance of the ships and establishments of the naval service, including the Royal Canadian navy, the Royal Canadian naval reesrve and the Royal Canadian naval volunteer reserve, $2,250,000.
Would the minister give an explanation of the increase?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The increase is for the Royal Canadian navy, no increase being provided for the other naval services. In order to meet the increased cost of pay and allowances for the Royal Canadian navy it has been necessary to increase their vote by the sum of $39,750, and the medical vote has also been increased by $3,000. The vote for miscellaneous effective service has been increased by $8,050 and for non-effective by $800. So that the net increase authorized may not exceed $28,000. The stores and allowances vote has been decreased by $23,600, bringing the net increase to $28,000.
The explanation of the reason for the increase in this year's estimates is that there are three engineering midshipmen doing courses at Keyham while last year there was only one. Additional officers in this branch, as the hon. member will recall, are badly needed. There is another cadet under training, there
being six instead of five. There is a long torpedo course for 1935-36, there being no such course in the past year. An additional torpedo officer was urgently required, there being no officer available until the present year. Other courses were estimated for last year and are to be carried out in the present year.
The minister has said there is an increased cost for pay and allowances amounting to $39,750. Are there any increases in individual amounts of pay?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Only in cases where promotion would carry with it the pay of a higher rank.

Would the minister inform me if there is any possible way for a young French Canadian, for instance, of about sixteen or seventeen years of age to join the Royal Canadian navy or the cadet school? What steps must be taken if he desires to follow that course?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Does the hon. member refer to an executive rank?
To start from the bottom as a cadet, if necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: As an officer?
As an officer, if possible, or even as a seaman.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Two different answers would be given, and I should like to know which the hon. member wishes.
As an officer.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: There are two ways of getting into the Royal Canadian navy, one after being accepted in the Royal Military College at Kingston where the cadet would spend two years and if successful would be chosen for entry into the Royal Canadian navy, and the other by taking a naval examination open to all Canada.
When and where do the examinations take place?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
They take place in
different Canadian centres. The applicant must not be older than eighteen and one-half years or younger than seventeen years.

I know that
graduates of the universities and seminaries of the province of Quebec with the degree of bachelor of arts or bachelor of science are admitted to the Royal Military college without further examination. Would the same apply to our naval academy?

Supply-Defence-Naval Services

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No, the applicant would have to take an examination, if I follow the hon. member correctly.

At what time of
the year would he apply?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The application ought
to be sent in by this time for the examination to be held in May.

Of what is the navy
composed at the present time? Where is it? Do you ever get it out of the garage?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: There are two destroyers on each coast.
What are their names?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The Skeena and the
Vancouver on the Pacific coast, together with the Armentieres, a mine sweeper, and on the Atlantic coast we have the Saguenay and the Champlain.

What services if
any have been performed by these cruisers during the past year?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Torpedo boat destroyers?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
At the present time
their services are largely those of training. They take the trips necessary to keep the ships' companies up to the mark in training. Also at this time of the year they join with the home fleet when the fleet of Great Britain comes into West Indian waters. To that point our two destroyers from each coast proceed. The destroyers on the Atlantic coast proceed directly to one of the more northern West Indian islands, and the two destroyers from the Pacific coast come down through the Panama canal to that rendezvous. They spend so many weeks together carrying out tactical exercises, gunnery, torpedo drills and manoeuvres, both by day and by night.
Do the ships passing through the Panama canal pay the tolls, the same as the liners?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes, the destroyers pay the usual toll.

Have they any
specific duty in connection with patrolling the coast?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
There is what is known as the Bamfield patrol on the western coast. I do not know that I can outline any specific duties; as a matter of fact I do not just know what the hon. member means by the term "sipecific duties." Undoubtedly they do

patrol the coast and if they were to discover something which was not carried on properly they would make adequate report to the authorities.

Is there any connection between the work of these ships and the work of any other department? For instance, on the Atlantic coast we have the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Is there any specific work in connection with the defence of the coast which they are regularly called upon to perform?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
There is no police or
detective work. I can only repeat what I said formerly, namely, that if trouble existed or an occasion arose they would act. Instances have occurred where ships of the Royal Canadian navy have been able to render considerable service to isolated dwellers along our coast. They have been able to give service also to distressed shipping. But with regard to definite patrols for a certain purpose other than just patrolling the coast and carrying out the training, I know of no such definite operations.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Royal Canadian Air Force-expenses in connection with the general maintenance and training of the permanent and non-permanent active air force, and provision of facilities therefor, $2,630,000.
I think the minister should make a statement with regard to this item, because there is a very substantial insr-ase.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
There is an increase of $700,000 in the Royal Canadian Air Force vote. I think it is obvious that in the national defence force which Canada indulges in, the three branches of the service take their certain place; they are proportionate one to the other. There has been a considerable increase of interest the world over in the force in the air, and these forces in the air have modulated their operations in conjunction with the forces of the sea and the forces of the land. Aviation, and particularly the air forces of the various nations, has developed with very great rapidity not only as a result of the experience of the war but as a result of aviation experience generally since the war, and consequently increases for aviation, provided the force which is being considered is to be kept really up to date, are in some ways more considerable than those for the sea service and the land service. Some few years after the war, reorganization of the Royal Canadian Air Force was planned. It has not been possible in these years of difficulty to keep up the: increase which was

Supply-Defence-Air Force
started prior to the depression for the purpose of obtaining that nucleus development which in, the interests of national defence it was considered desirable that the forces should have so far as the air was concerned. This year an attempt is being made to catch up some of that slack, to move a little further towards the attainment of the desirable quantity of machines and personnel which are required to put the Royal Canadian Air Force into its proper relation to the other defence forces in the country.

Would the minister give us some idea of what he considers the desirable force? He mentioned a little earlier plans for a certain establishment that was thought desirable. What has the minister or the department in mind as to the force considered desirable in this country?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: This estimate provides for a strength of 969 permanent and 526 nonpermanent air force personnel, compared with 785 permanent and 399 non-permanent provided for the previous year. I do not know if that answers the hon. gentleman's question.

No, it does not go far enough. If I understood the minister aright, he said he had larger plans in view and that this was a step in the direction of that larger plan. I should like to know what is that larger plan. What is considered the desirable air force that we should have in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I am not in a position to lay down here to-night what perhaps the hon. gentleman is thinking of, the ultimate aim of Canada in the air. I cannot give it. Probably plans and arrangements will have to be modified as the years go by.

I am just taking the minister's own statement a few minutes ago when he said that the department had a certain force in view as desirable for Canada. I take it that there must foe some plan, some definite establishment which the minister would like to see created, and that this is one step in that direction.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I am not aware that that is in the form of a list which could be read off. Certainly I have not got it here.

Has the minister information before him regarding the number of sites that have been or are about to be purchased for airports and landing fields? In a return that I received the other day I was very much surprised to see the number of sites purchased in British Columbia. Is that policy being carried out throughout the whole of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: To answer the hon. member in detail would take a little time.
I do not want it in detail, but has the minister the amount that has been expended or is to 'be expended on sites for airports and landing fields?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I cannot pick that out now, certainly, but of course in regard to the sites which have been worked on under relief measures, for instance, a very considerable number of them have been acquired without the expenditure of money. Some have been transferred from the interior department and some have been taken over by arrangement with the province concerned. I think that comparatively few pieces of land had to be purchased for the purpose.
Perhaps an answer to this question will serve my purpose. Is the department carrying out a policy of purchasing sites for airports and landing fields throughout Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes, the department certainly is making a gesture towards the day when Canada will have dotted right across this country from coast to coast aerodromes, airports and emergency landing fields. But that is in the future, certainly not in the present.
Is the department paying for airports in cities? I do not think so.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
No, but the department is endeavouring to see to it that there are emergency landing fields right across Canada, the total distance being divided up, if I remember rightly, into distances averaging thirty-five miles apart. The problem of a trans-Canada airway has been engaging the study of the aviation branch of the department for several years, and its development was commenced in 1927. In 1930 thirty landing fields had been established and equipped for night flying, the section traversing the prairie provinces being practically completed. Lack of funds prevented further development and necessitated the discontinuance of the inter-city air services of Winnipeg-Leth-bridge-Edmonton and Toronto-Winnipeg. In anticipation of improved financial conditions the aviation branch is continuing to watch closely the development of air transportation in other countries in its various forms.
Supply-Defence-Air Force

The minister has indicated that he is not able to state the objectives which are sought to be reached in connection with personnel and machines. Could he tell us the present personnel of the Canadian air force, that is officers and other ranks, and then tell us what addition to this personnel is contemplated?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: There will be an increase of seventeen officers and 167 men.

And the number of
machines?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The purchases which will be required under this estimate are four fighter type, ten training type and seven bombing type machines.
Is it expected that these machines will be purchased in England?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: If the requisite machines can be obtained in Canada, it will be desirable to obtain them here. This is a matter of close examination of all factors.

I think the force and
the country are primarily interested in training machines. There is much difference of opinion as to what type of training machine is desirable and I should like to know if the department has arrived at a definite conclusion as to what type will be purchased.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
In the past we have
kept in close touch with the Royal Air Force and many machines have been purchased from that organization. Others have been purchased from other sources. I am not in position to say that a definite decision has been arrived at as to the type of training planes to be purchased.

Does the minister contemplate taking on at least some of the men who were dropped two or three years ago at the time the drastic reductions were made in the force? I believe about eighty officers were let out.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: It is the intention of the department to consider the applications of those men who were let out for purposes of economy, but it must be remembered that a younger type of man is coming along ready to start at the bottom.

There used to be a system of summer courses for college students carried on at Camp Borden. Are these being continued, either at Camp Borden or at Trenton? How many students are expected to take these courses?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: In ab initio flying, eleven officers and four other ranks; instrument flying, Trenton and Ottawa, three officers and three other ranks; air pilotage, Camp Borden, three officers; army cooperation Camp Borden, ten officers; for army officers, fifteen officers; flying instructors, Camp Borden, four officers and squadron armament, Camp Borden, four officers and three other ranks.
What I was asking about were the Camp Borden courses. I should like to know how many will be taking those courses.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Eleven officers and four
other ranks.

speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Civil Aviation-
Expenses in connection with the control of civil aviation, airways, government and public air ports and grants to aeroplane clubs, $250,000.

I notice that the British government has decided recently to separate civil aviation from military flying. I should like to quote an article which appeared in the Spectator of December 21, as follows:
Recent decisions show that the government is now fully alive to the necessity of freeing civil aviation from the dominance of military aviation, and of a more vigorous policy in conjunction with the dominions for the development of commercial air routes within the empire. The air council henceforward will be concerned exclusively with the military side. The Director of Civil Aviation will become Director-General, and will take decisions in conjunction with the Secretary of State and the Under-Secretary. Expenditure on civil flying will have to be judged independently of military expenditure, and on its merits. The hope must be that international agreements will admit of the enlargement of the civil vote through the reduction of the military. If we are to hold our own in competition with foreign countries, ground organization must be improved and regular services must be quickened. To no small extent the future cohesion of the empire depends on the air-not on the air force, but on the efficiency of civil services.
If such a decision has been arrived at in England, it seems to me highly desirable that we should proceed along somewhat similar lines. Perhaps this would be even more desirable in Canada than in England because we are so closely in touch with the American air routes. If civil flying is to be developed to the extent to which it should be developed, we should not be tied up with military operations. Has the minister's department given consideration to this matter, and is it prepared to recommend to the government action along these lines?

Supply-Defence-Radio

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I do not consider that any division other than exists at present is required in this country. There is no connection between civil aviation and the Royal Canadian Air Force; they are two separate branches. True, they come under the one minister, but they are entirely separate.

Is it necessary that they should come under the military arm? I do not see how the minister can say that they are quite separate, because a few minutes ago he suggested that there should be the closest cooperation with regard to landing fields and so on, and in the training of pilots I think the two are closely connected. At any rate, that is my information.

I am afraid I do not follow the hon. member. One might as well argue, it seems to me, that a man who drives a taxicab is not the same type of individual as the man who drives a motor ambulance. They are the same type of individual, they have to perform the same sort of operation; but there is no connection between the two. Both types might have to use the same airfield or seadrome and they both fly airplanes. They both know something of the design of machines and engines, but I do not see how they are connected.
In the first place, this comes under the military department. That is the first and essential thing we are discussing to-night.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: They happen to come under one minister but they are not related in any other sense.
Are we not discussing the affairs of the Department of National Defence, or have we passed entirely from the Department of National Defence?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: This is civil aviation.

Yes, but it comes
under the Department of National Defence.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: It comes under this minister, who happens to be Minister of National Defence.

If I understand
rightly, in England there will be provision to take it completely out of the Department of National Defence, making some other arrangement.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Perhaps Canada will do the same some day.

I have asked the
minister whether consideration has been given to the idea of taking it out of the Department of Defence.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I cannot say that I
have given it consideration. Obviously the day may come when all sorts of changes will be made within these departments, but at present I am not giving consideration to civil aviation doing anything but remaining where it is.

To emphasize the fact
that there are civil activities in this military department, may I as a last word bring to the attention of the minister the matter of having, if possible, an airplane located on the eastern coast of Halifax for the benefit of navigation during the winter months?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: At Dartmouth?

Well, that is-across the
harbour. I have already brought it to the minister's attention, and other repn-a stations have been made to him. It is well worthy of consideration. It would have done valiant service if it had been located there last winter during the excessive storms; it would have assisted in locating a ship that was adrift for between twenty-four and I'oriwi . hours. Has the minister come to any conclusion in the matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: It has not been definitely decided, but it is under close oh- muon and a decision will be arrived at. shortly.

There will not be a
department of communications this year?

Will it be finished in
